Subject: Private GPU pool — capacity & safety matrix review

Hi Olivia / Ben,

Thanks again for the workshop yesterday. Per our conversation, I put together an initial sizing and safety matrix for the on‑prem GPU pool you plan to run in your primary data hall. The attached spreadsheet (sizing_matrix_v1.xlsx) contains the simulation inputs; I also included a CSV export of the simulator runs. Key outputs and assumptions are below — please treat these as a recommended starting point for the pilot.

High level goals:
- Steady throughput target: 5k tokens/sec (aggregate across workers) for peak 95th percentile traffic.
- Burst allowance: up to 25k tokens/sec sustained for 90s windows (backstopped by graceful degradation policies).
- Latency SLO: 95th token latency <= 120ms for chat-style traffic with 1024 context.

Sizing mapping (model / quantization / recommended GPUs for steady):
- llama-2-70b (q8_0) — 12 x 80GB GPUs for steady 5k tps; warm+burst headroom requires 16 GPUs
- redwood-7b-rlhf (q4f) — 3 x 40GB-class GPUs for 5k tps; 4 for burst headroom
- opt-13b (q4) — 6 x 80GB GPUs for steady; 8 for safe burst

Notes on what drives these numbers:
- KV cache pressure and peak sequence length are the single biggest cost when modeling chat workloads. The spreadsheet includes two scenarios (avg seq 256, heavy seq 1024) — plan to size for the heavier unless you can enforce strict truncation.
- Network egress and cross-rack bandwidth: every additional GPU adds ~350–450 MB/s of P2P traffic in our simulation for large KV cache syncs. If your racks are limited (<=25Gbps inter-rack), that will throttle useful parallelism.
- Warm pools: to meet the burst allowance without cold-start spikes we recommend keeping 10–20% of GPUs hot as a warm pool depending on model size (column F in the spreadsheet).

Operational safety matrix (short):
- Safety headroom: recommend 30–40% headroom for managed clusters with unpredictable traffic; reduce to 20% only with strong request shaping.
- Autoscaler policy: predictive scale-up (based on rolling token rate + queue depth) with aggressive scale-down cooldown (8–12m) to avoid oscillation.
- Fallbacks: route 20% of overflow traffic to Redwood hosted endpoints (controlled via routing policy) if private capacity is saturated.

Next steps I propose:
1) Can you confirm the exact GPU inventory and cross-rack bandwidth per rack? I used a conservative 25Gbps figure where not supplied.
2) If you want, we can schedule a 90-minute sizing workshop where Dev can run a quick sim live and walk through the warm-pool tradeoffs.

Attachments: sizing_matrix_v1.xlsx (sim inputs + tolerances), sim_results_private_pool_20261212.csv

Thanks,
Aditya Rao

Team —

Quick internal thread following Olivia's reply. Action items and recommended adjustments:

1) Run a 10x A100 simulation (25Gbps fabric, no RDMA). Dev — can you run that with the same workload profile (95th token rate target 5k, burst 25k/90s) and export the CSV? Prioritize the heavy seq=1024 scenario.

2) Safety margin change: with only 10 GPUs available I recommend we set operational headroom to 40% and lean on more aggressive request shaping & early rejection on tail latencies. That means steady-serving capacity aimed at ~3.5k tps and a burst policy that tops at ~10–12k tps with graceful degradation to hosted endpoints.

3) Network mitigation recommendations (share with Acme infra):
- MTU 9000 across the rack and enable LRO/TSO to reduce CPU/NIC overhead for large KV syncs.
- If they can enable RoCE or at least prioritized QoS for P2P traffic, we can get noticeable gains — but treat this as optional for pilot.
- Keep cross-rack RPCs minimized; prefer intra-rack placement for the models we expect to scale horizontally.

4) Warm pool / cold-start: propose 2 hot GPUs reserved as warm standby for the largest model in the pool; this reduces cold-start latency and prevents the 95th latency spikes during short bursts.

5) Fallback behavior: we will implement an explicit routing policy mapping: when local queue depth exceeds threshold X, route new requests to Redwood hosted model variants with no KV sync and model-dropping heuristics. We will only forward request metadata and truncated context for safety; full customer data never leaves on failed requests unless they opt-in. (Need legal / security confirmation but this is our default pattern.)

6) Cost/contract note: for a pilot using 10 GPUs + 2 warm standby (logical warm reserve), estimate monthly infra equivalent cost and provide optional temporary dedicated capacity on Redwood hosted for overflow (quote to follow). Marissa — can you draft the preliminary cost delta for a 3-month pilot with the fallback reserve enabled?

Dev — handing off the sim run to you. Aim to have the 10‑GPU CSV and a small slide deck summarizing the headroom tradeoffs by EOD Monday.

Thanks,
Aditya

Hi Olivia / Ben —

Thanks for the quick clarifications. We ran the 10x A100 simulation (attached CSV) under the heavy sequence scenario and 25Gbps cross‑rack fabric. Short summary of the results and the recommended pilot configuration below. Full simulation results and the revised sizing sheet are attached.

Summary (10 x A100 pilot):
- Recommended steady configuration: allocate 8 GPUs to serving (allocated across a single rack to minimize cross-rack P2P), 2 GPUs as warm standby for the largest model. This maps to ~3.6k steady tps under heavy sequences (95th percentile).
- Burst behavior: with aggressive request shaping and priority queuing we can expose short bursts up to ~11–12k tps for ~60–90s before quality-targeted fallbacks route overflow to Redwood hosted endpoints.
- Network risk: under this configuration cross-rack uplink approaches 75–80% utilization during simulated bursts. Enabling MTU 9000 / LRO reduced observed CPU overhead in the sim by ~18% and lowered queueing jitter. Enabling RoCE would further reduce tail latency but is not required for the pilot.
- Latency SLO: 95th token latency ~115ms in the sim; tail spikes beyond that were correlated with cold-starts for the large model and with cross-rack retransmits. Warm standby mitigated the cold starts.

Data residency / fallback specifics:
- Fallback routing will send only truncated request context and non-sensitive metadata to the Redwood hosted endpoint when local thresholds are reached. No persistent logs or full request payloads will be sent without explicit opt-in. We'll put the precise fields that can be forwarded in a short dataflow doc and share it with your security team before enabling fallback.

Next steps / asks:
1) Please confirm you are OK with the 8+2 topology for the pilot.
2) If you want us to attempt cross-rack optimizations, acme-infra should enable MTU 9000 and QoS for P2P traffic; we can give them a short checklist (attached network-checklist.pdf).
3) Marissa will send a 3‑month pilot cost estimate and an optional Redwood overflow reserve quote.
4) Schedule: propose a 90-minute runbook workshop on Wed (Dec 16) — please confirm availability.

Attachments: sim_results_private_pool_20261212.csv, sizing_matrix_v1_revised.xlsx, network-checklist.pdf

Thanks — happy to jump on a call to walk through the CSV and tradeoffs live.
